newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Jail terms sought in S.Korean graft scandal.
newsitem.headline: Jail terms sought in S.Korean graft scandal.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors on Monday demanded long jail terms for the founder of the Hanbo Group and top bankers and politicians standing trial with him in a graft scandal that has rocked the nation.
They called for a 20-year prison sentence for Chung Tae-soo, the founder of the nation's 14th largest business group, and six years for his son, Kim Bo-keun, the current chairman.
Father and son have been charged with bribery and embezzlement in connection with the collapse in January of the group's steelmaking flagship under five trillion won ($5.6 billion) in debts.
Prosecutors allege that the elder Chung scattered cash among bankers and politicians to keep loans rolling in to his stricken Hanbo Steel Co.
The politicians, among them three top aides to president Kim Young-sam, are accused of influence-peddling to guarantee funding for a massive new steel mill.
"This is a large scale corruption case perpetrated by a collaboration of immoral politicians, bankers and corporate executives," prosecutor Park San-gil told the court.
"It has even damaged the nation's reputation."
He said the 74-year-old Hanbo founder "ignored the minimum of corporate and social ethics".
Prosecutors demanded a six-year jail term for former Home Affairs minister Kim Woo-suk.

The asked for 7-1/2 years for ruling New Korea Party lawmaker Hong In-gil, five years each for two other ruling party lawmakers, Hwang Byung-tai and Chung Jae-chull, and seven years for Kwon Roh-kap, a prominent lawmaker with the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
They requested seven years each for the former president of Korea First Bank, Sheen Kwang-shik, and the onetime head of the Chohung Bank, Woo Chan-mok.
For another former Korea First president, Rhee Chul-soo, they called for an eight-year term.
In addition, prosecutors asked the Seoul District Criminal Court to jail for five years the former financial controller of the Hanbo Group, Kim Jong-kook.
Earlier, a Seoul court issued an arrest warrant on graft charges for a former intelligence chief close to the disgraced son of president Kim Young-sam.
Kim Ki-sup will be charged with taking 150 million won in kickbacks and influence-peddling.

State prosecutors had sought the warrant on Sunday. They accuse Kim Ki-sup of accepting the money from a former top executive of Daeho Construction Co in return for help obtaining a lucrative cable television licence.
The president's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, who was arrested and held in detention on Saturday, was also charged with taking bribes from the businessman, Lee Sung-ho.
Kim Ki-sup resigned as deputy director of the Agency for National Security Planning as the Hanbo scandal unfolded. He has denied taking bribes.
Opposition parties accuse him of managing around seven billion won of unspent funds from president Kim's 1992 election campaign at the request of Kim Hyun-chul.
Alleged political slush funds have become a burning political issue, and President Kim is under growing pressure to give a full public account of his campaign financing.
The president, whose image as a graft-fighter has been shattered by the Hanbo loans-for-kickbacks scandal, is expected to make an announcement on the subject on Wednesday. ($1=891 won)
